title: the owl and the crows
hookLine: two men sleep under a banyan tree, and the third lies awake watching an owl hunt
carry: from anger comes confusion, the Gita warns

cards: A huge banyan tree in a forest at night, its branches full of sleeping crows. Under it, three tired warriors have stopped to rest. They've ridden away from the field, afraid the Pandavas might find them.
Kripa lies down and sleeps. Kritavarma sleeps too; they've been fighting for days. But Ashvatthama can't sleep.
He lies on the ground with his eyes open, burning, the text says, with anger and grief. And up in the branches, something moves.

teach.b: In Ganguli's telling, an owl comes down through the dark, large and fierce, with sharp talons, and lands among the sleeping crows. One by one, it kills them. The crows never wake in time to fly.
Ashvatthama watches the whole thing, and says to himself, in effect: this owl has taught me something. The Pandavas can't be beaten in open battle. But tonight they'll be asleep.
Notice: no god speaks, no adviser plots. The owl only hunted. It was Ashvatthama who made it a plan.

Hindus know a well-known teaching about exactly this. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna traces a ladder downward. Brooding on a thing brings attachment; attachment brings desire; desire, blocked, turns to anger.
From anger comes confusion. From confusion, memory slips. And when memory slips, buddhi, the power to judge, is lost, and with it the person.
Many readers watch Ashvatthama go down that ladder under the banyan: grief, then anger, then a mind that can no longer tell a sign from a wish.
For us, it's the hour after midnight, when a hurt feels like proof and everything seems to point to the thing you already wanted to do. The Gita's answer isn't to stop feeling.
It's to notice which rung you're on, and not to decide anything there.

how: The owl among the crows appears in retellings and illustrated editions of the Mahabharata when they tell the night raid.

games.q: you're Ashvatthama, lying awake under the banyan, sure the owl has shown you the way. by the Gita's teaching, what's the wise move?
o: decide now, while the plan feels so clear.
wait for morning and a clearer mind before deciding anything.
trust the owl; a sign like that can't be wrong.
games.why: the Gita warns that anger clouds buddhi, judgment. Ashvatthama decides in the dark, and wakes the others with his mind already made up.

practice: Many Hindu families end the day with a short prayer, offering up the day and asking forgiveness for whatever went wrong in it, by hand, by word or by thought. Let your shoulders go heavy and your jaw loose.
Bring to mind one thought that keeps you awake. Breathing out, hand it over for the night: to God, if you pray, or simply to the morning, when you can judge it with a clear head.

wordCard.voice: Sauptika. The night book: a banyan, sleeping crows, an owl, and one man awake who lets anger read the owl as a lesson.
